text: If you can't fall asleep without the TV on, it might not be the noise you need. It might be what the silence makes you feel.
It's eleven forty-seven p.m. Maya turns off the TV, closes her eyes... and her brain immediately starts talking.
That email she forgot to send. The rent. The weird thing she said in a meeting... three years ago.
So she turns the TV back on. Some show she's seen a hundred times. Fifteen minutes later, she's out cold.
Maya isn't a real person. But if you're watching this, there's a good chance her night is your night.
So let's follow her, hour by hour, and answer three questions: why does the TV work so well, is it actually bad for you, and what can you do instead?
And stay until the end: I'll share six simple things you can try tonight, with or without the TV.
First, a quick guess. How many Americans watch TV in the last hour before bed, almost every night?
In a national sleep poll, it was about two out of three baby boomers, and about half of younger adults.
So no, you're not weird. You're completely normal.
Eleven forty-eight. Why silence is so loud.
Here's the first surprise: your brain doesn't switch off when you stop doing things. It switches channels.
The moment the world goes quiet, a network in your brain takes over. Scientists call it the default mode network. Think of it as your brain's screensaver.
It's the same system behind shower thoughts. It replays conversations, plans tomorrow, and digs up that embarrassing moment from seventh grade.
During the day, noise and people drown it out. But in a dark, silent bedroom, nothing competes with it. It plays at full volume.
Quick question: what's the first thing your brain replays when the room goes quiet? Tell me in the comments. I bet it's something embarrassing.
How much do we hate being alone with our thoughts? Researchers actually tested it.
They left people alone in an empty room for fifteen minutes. No phone. Nothing to do but think.
There was just one button, and it gave a mild electric shock. A shock they had already tried, and said they would pay money to avoid.
Two out of three men pressed it anyway. One man pressed it one hundred ninety times. Some people would literally rather get shocked than sit alone with their mind.
Now imagine that, at midnight. That's the silence Maya is running from.
Midnight. Why the TV works so well.
Picture your brain like a web browser that can only keep about four tabs open at once.
In silence, worries grab all four: work, money, that text you never answered, tomorrow's alarm.
A TV show steals a few of those tabs. A simple story, some voices, a little laughter. Your worries don't disappear. They just lose their seats.
And notice what Maya picks. Not a new crime thriller. The same comfort show she's seen a hundred times.
That's not laziness. A new show keeps your brain on alert: who did it, what happens next? A rerun has no cliffhanger. You already know every joke and every ending.
So your brain can safely let go in the middle, because it won't miss a thing.
There's another hidden trick. Sleep is one of the only things that gets harder the more you try.
Ever noticed you can doze off on the couch in five minutes... but lie awake for an hour in bed? Same effect.
In one experiment, people who were told to fall asleep as fast as possible, while their minds were busy, actually took longer than people who weren't pushed.
The TV takes the pressure off. Maya isn't trying to sleep. She's just watching. And that's exactly when sleep sneaks up on her.
But for many people, the biggest reason isn't the story. It's the voices.
Our brains are wired to notice human voices. And with characters we know well, we form one-sided friendships. Psychologists call them parasocial relationships.
In one study, people who had just written about a fight with someone close felt less hurt after writing about their favorite TV show. The show worked a little like a friend.
So for someone who lives alone, or whose partner is already asleep, the TV isn't noise. It's company.
Some researchers think something even older is going on.
For most of human history, soft voices nearby meant your group was close, and someone was keeping watch. Total silence could mean you were alone.
It's only a theory. But it fits how so many people describe it: silence feels exposed, and soft voices feel safe.
Two forty-seven a.m. What the TV does while you sleep.
Here's the catch. Maya falls asleep. The TV doesn't.
Surprise number two: your eyelids are not blackout curtains. Some light gets through, and your eyes have special cells whose main job is to tell your body clock whether it's day or night.
And a TV isn't a steady night-light. It flashes from dark scenes to bright ones all night long.

In a Northwestern University study, healthy young adults slept just one night with the room lights on. Their heart rate stayed higher during sleep, and the next morning, their bodies handled sugar less well. After one night.
That study used ceiling lights, not a TV. But it shows your sleeping body is still watching the light.
And if you're thinking, at least it's not my phone... you're half right.

A phone held a foot from your face sends far more light into your eyes than a TV across the room. In a Harvard sleep lab study, people who read on a glowing e-reader before bed took longer to fall asleep, and felt groggier the next morning, than people who read a printed book.
So if you have to choose, the TV across the room beats the phone in your face.
Another study followed more than forty thousand women for about five years. Those who slept with a TV or a light on were more likely to gain eleven pounds or more.
That doesn't prove the TV caused it. Other habits could explain part of it. But it's one more reason sleep scientists keep saying the same thing: darkness matters.
Then there's the sound. At two forty-seven, a commercial comes on, suddenly louder than the show. A laugh track. A door slams on screen.

Maya doesn't wake up. But her brain hears it. Noise during sleep can cause tiny arousals: little jolts that speed up the heart and pull you out of deep sleep for a few seconds, without you ever remembering.
That's how you can spend eight hours in bed with the TV on, and still wake up exhausted.
And here's something most people don't know: you don't sleep in one long block.

Every night, you go through four to six cycles of about ninety minutes: light sleep, deep sleep, then dreaming sleep. And between cycles, everyone wakes up for a moment, several times a night. Usually, you roll over and forget it.
But if the TV is blasting a commercial at that exact moment, a few seconds can turn into a real wake-up.
At three twelve a.m., Maya opens her eyes, watches ten minutes of an infomercial... and it takes her half an hour to fall back asleep.
Six thirty a.m. So, is it actually bad?
The alarm rings. Maya feels like she barely slept, and the TV is still on, asking if she's still watching.
There's also a habit loop at play. The brain learns what the bed is for. If bed means TV, after enough nights, silence doesn't just feel hard. It feels wrong.
So here's the honest answer: falling asleep to the TV isn't the big problem. Most of the downsides come from leaving it on all night: the light, the noise, the hours it keeps running.
And sometimes it's worth asking a deeper question. Lonely people tend to sleep about as long as everyone else, but their sleep is more broken.
So if the TV feels like company, maybe what you're really missing... is company.
And if you have kids, pediatricians recommend keeping TVs and phones out of their bedrooms, and turning screens off about an hour before bed.
A bedtime story gives them what the TV gives so many adults: a calm voice, and company.
What Maya tried instead.
So what did Maya change? Not everything at once. Here's what actually helps, according to sleep research. This isn't medical advice, just what has been tested.
One: keep the voice, lose the light. A podcast, an audiobook, or a TV with the screen turned off gives you the company without the glow.
Two: set a sleep timer. Thirty minutes is usually plenty. You get the help falling asleep, without five hours of flashing light and sudden noise.
Three: if you need sound all night, pick a steady one.
A fan, rain, or white noise doesn't change, so it can actually cover sudden noises instead of creating them.
Four, and this one surprised researchers: write tomorrow's to-do list.
In a sleep lab study, people who spent five minutes writing a to-do list fell asleep about nine minutes faster than people who wrote about what they'd already done.
Once it's on paper, your brain can stop rehearsing it.
Five: try this with me, right now. Breathe in through your nose.
Now take a second, small breath in, on top of the first one.
And breathe out, slowly... all the way.
That's called cyclic sighing. In a Stanford study, five minutes a day of it lifted people's mood more than mindfulness meditation.
And if you're still awake after about twenty minutes, get up. Do something calm in dim light, and come back when you feel sleepy. That keeps your bed linked to sleep, not to frustration.
Don't go cold turkey. Shorten the timer a little each week. And if you lie awake most nights for weeks, talk to a doctor. Insomnia is common, and it's very treatable.
Three weeks later, Maya still puts something on at night. But now it's a podcast with a timer, in a dark room. Most nights, she's asleep before it ends.
Because the TV was never the real problem. It was her brain's solution: a way to quiet the noise inside, and feel a little less alone.
So be honest: do you sleep with the TV on? And what do you watch? Tell me in the comments.
